aliases.name: テケテケ
aliases.meaning: Onomatopoeic 'teke teke' for the scratching/scuttling sound she makes

aliases.name: Kashima Reiko
aliases.meaning: Closely related Japanese urban-legend figure of a girl whose legs were severed by a train, often treated as a precursor to the Teke Teke legend

description.summary: A Japanese urban-legend onryō: the spirit of a young woman or schoolgirl bisected by a train who travels on her hands or elbows, making a 'teke-teke' scratching sound, and bisects those she catches.
description.full: Teke Teke (テケテケ) is a Japanese urban legend that emerged in the 1980s and reached peak popularity in the 1990s. The legend tells of an onryō — a vengeful ghost — formed when a young woman or schoolgirl fell from a railway platform and was cut in two by an oncoming train. In most retellings she dies because of inadequate response by station staff and bystanders. Now lacking the lower half of her body, she travels on her hands or elbows at extremely high speed, dragging her bisected torso along the ground and producing a scratching sound rendered onomatopoeically as 'teke teke teke teke'. Encountering her at night, especially in train stations, school grounds, or empty streets, allegedly leads to pursuit; if she catches a victim, she severs them at the waist with a scythe or similar implement, perpetuating the cycle. Teke Teke is closely related to the older urban legend of Kashima Reiko, a girl in Hokkaidō traditionally said to have lost her legs in a railway accident; both legends share a railway-trauma origin. A Japanese horror film, 'Teketeke', was released in 2009, with a sequel the same year. The legend belongs to a broader cluster of Japanese urban-legend ghosts (kuchisake-onna, Hanako-san, aka manto) that became cultural touchstones in late-20th-century Japan.

etymology.origin: Japanese onomatopoeia 'teke teke', the scratching or scuttling sound she is said to make as she pulls her body along the ground.
etymology.meaning: Approximately 'scratch-scratch' — naming the entity after the sound of her movement.
etymology.first_use: 1980s schoolyard urban legends in Japan; popularised in the 1990s in tabloids and television.

related_phenomena.name: Kashima Reiko
related_phenomena.description: Older Japanese urban legend of a legless ghost in railway/bathroom contexts; precursor to Teke Teke

related_phenomena.name: Kuchisake-onna (Slit-Mouthed Woman)
related_phenomena.description: Contemporary Japanese urban-legend onryō pursuing schoolchildren

related_phenomena.name: Hanako-san
related_phenomena.description: Japanese urban-legend ghost said to haunt school bathrooms

features.description: Lacks the lower half; the torso ends at the waist, dragging exposed organs and clothing
Travels by pulling herself along the ground using her arms, producing the characteristic 'teke teke' scratching sound
Many versions equip her with a scythe, sickle, or similar tool with which she bisects victims
Most retellings dress her in a Japanese school uniform; some give an OL (office lady) appearance

physical.morphology: Onryō (vengeful ghost) class entity; appears as a young woman whose body has been severed at the waist.

abilities.description: Despite being legless, she moves faster than a sprinting human, cited as a defining horror element of the legend
Cuts those she catches in two at the waist, often turning them into new Teke Teke
Announces her approach with a 'teke teke' scraping sound

patterns: Targets young women and schoolchildren in many retellings
Self-perpetuating: victims who survive bisection become new Teke Teke in some variants

range.description: Originally a Japanese schoolyard / tabloid urban legend; widely diffused since the 2000s through Japanese horror media and English-language internet culture.

first_recorded.source: Japanese schoolyard urban legends, recorded in 1980s–1990s tabloid and TV coverage

peak_activity_periods.description: Urban-legend boom in Japanese popular culture
Two films, 'Teketeke' and 'Teketeke 2', anchor the legend in J-horror

origins.cultural_roots: Late-20th-century Japanese urban folklore, drawing on the wider yūrei (ghost) tradition and on real anxieties around railway accidents in modernising Japan.
origins.earliest_accounts: Schoolyard and magazine retellings in 1980s Japan; the 'Kashima Reiko' precursor is older.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to the wider gakkō no kaidan ('school ghost stories') boom of the 1990s, of which kuchisake-onna and Hanako-san are the most famous figures.

timeline.event: Teke Teke and related Kashima Reiko legends are in active oral and print circulation in Japan
timeline.significance: Anchor period of the legend's emergence

timeline.event: Japanese horror film 'Teketeke', directed by Kōji Shiraishi, is released in Japan
timeline.significance: Major film treatment that helped diffuse the legend internationally
Cements the legend in J-horror franchises

history.modern_era: The Teke Teke legend remains active in Japanese horror media (film, manga, anime, video games) and in English-language internet horror communities, where it appears in urban-legend lists and in adapted creepypasta retellings.

documentary.name: Teketeke (2009 film)
documentary.description: Japanese horror film directed by Kōji Shiraishi based on the Teke Teke legend.
documentary.analysis: Major film adaptation; primary 21st-century vehicle for the legend.

documentary.name: Teketeke 2 (2009 film)
documentary.analysis: Cements the legend in J-horror franchise output.

skeptical.name: Modern urban legend
skeptical.description: Folklorists treat Teke Teke as a typical late-20th-century Japanese urban legend rather than as a paranormal report; its structure follows the schoolyard urban-legend pattern (rumour, ritual avoidance, transmission as warning).
evidence_cited: No documented witness reports treated as serious cryptozoological / parapsychological claims

traditions: Late-20th-century Japanese gakkō no kaidan (school ghost stories)
stories: Kashima Reiko's railway accident in Hokkaidō
Variants in which speaking the legend's name aloud invites Teke Teke to appear within a month unless the story is passed on
folklore.beliefs: Treated as a frightening urban legend used by schoolchildren; elements (chain-letter retelling, ritual avoidance phrases) function as classic urban-legend folkloric mechanisms.

literature: Inclusions in major Japanese urban-legend compendia (e.g., Tsunemitsu Tōru's 'Gakkō no kaidan')
film_tv: References on Japanese ghost-story anthology programmes (Honto ni atta kowai hanashi, etc.)
games: Used as a model for various indie horror games and internet-horror creepypasta adaptations

researchers.name: Tsunemitsu Tōru
researchers.contribution: Major scholarly compilation of Japanese school ghost stories ('Gakkō no kaidan')

research.ongoing_studies: Continuing scholarly interest in late-20th-century Japanese urban legends as a folklore phenomenon.
